mordant

/MOR-duhnt/ - the stress falls on MOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mordant means bitingly witty — humor or criticism with a dry, cutting edge meant to leave a mark.

The playwright's mordant curtain speech thanked the critics 'for attending in shifts,' and the line drew laughter and blood in equal measure.

Example

The staff cartoonist never raised her voice in the news meeting; she saved it for the page, where one mordant caption — the governor cutting a ribbon on a bridge to nowhere, labeled 'Progress' — did more damage than the editorial printed beside it.

Mordant is wit with teeth. It is quieter than scathing (this unit): a scathing verdict batters its target openly, while a mordant line amuses the room and lets the target feel the sting a beat later. And the sting is no accident — mordant humor is dry, deliberate, and precise, funny to everyone except the person bitten.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

caustic: Caustic criticism burns like the chemical it is named for — harsh, corrosive, and openly angry, with no obligation to amuse anyone. Mordant carries the same acid but delivers it as wit: the line entertains the room even as it bites its target.

barbed: A barbed remark is fitted with a hook — built to snag and sting on its way past. Mordant goes beyond the single barb: it is a whole manner of humor, dry and controlled, in which every joke carries its own point.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

good-natured: teasing that means no harm and leaves no sting

anodyne: so mild and inoffensive that no one could possibly be stung

Where it sits · how deep the humor's bite goes

wry → mordant → venomous

wry vs. mordant: Wry is milder than mordant: a wry aside raises one eyebrow at the mess and means no harm, while mordant wit bites down hard enough to leave a mark.

venomous vs. mordant: Venomous goes further than mordant: mordant humor still wants the laugh it earns, but a venomous line has stopped joking and exists only to poison and wound.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mord: to bite (Latin mordere)

Suffix — -ant: doing it now — a present-participle adjective ending

Put it together: Mord- (Latin mordere, 'to bite') + -ant (a present-participle ending: 'doing it now') = 'biting.' French used mordant for a dog that bites and kept it for wit that does the same, and English borrowed the figurative jaw whole. Mordere's bitten-down form mors- also survives in morsel and remorse — the root never stopped chewing on English.

Use the root in a new word: remorse: Sentenced at last, the swindler read a statement of remorse so polished that the judge doubted every word of it.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Mordant is the connoisseur's word for wit with teeth, and it is a scalpel rather than a bludgeon: dry, precise, never shouted. Curt and brusque (this unit) are about giving too few words; mordant is about what a few well-chosen words can do. Reserve it for humor, satire, and criticism — a mordant essay, a mordant aside — and note its day job: dyers and printers use mordant as a noun for the chemical that bites color into cloth, the same Latin teeth at honest work.
